The issue, as a lifelong Democrat, is pragmatism. Progressive ideas need really good execution to work. Fraud does exist. Mismanagement and waste does exist. Humans are flawed and a certain percent will try to cheat, steal, commit crimes, etc. The problem isn't the ideas it is how they are implemented. 

The amount of spending on the Homeless problem in Cali and NYC are good examples. Billions and billions mismanaged with almost no tangible progress to show for it. 

Defund the police another example- reforming the police needed to happen, but the pie-in-the-sky idea that society could function without enforcing laws and jailing people who commit violent crimes was a disaster. Look what happened when shoplifting was not enforced. No common sense.

Ezra Klein discusses the issue well. Democrats need to focus on tangible results. The idea/policy is often less important than the hard work of implementing these policies in practical and efficient ways!

comments.name: jeff cunningham
comments.body: Look, this is Phase II, not an extension of Phase I, and it has been building for a while. Trump desperately wanted a rational enemy, but Iran, being Iran, could not meet the spec. The crucial question is, where do we go from here? Iran has lost its ability to threaten its real adversaries, the US and Israel. Therefore, it applies pressure to the Gulf Kingdoms through Hormuz and/or infrastructure. Both of these measures can be managed, assuming that the electorate doesn’t change its wavering mind. Trump will contain Iran, causing it to bleed revenues and unsold oil, for as long as necessary. Stalemates are a preferable option to war, provided that it’s a war you’re confident you can win.  What worries me is Israel. Their more existential vulnerability is not reduced by stalemate (they've been living with that for decades). I'm guessing they have a sortee or two in their playbook to wipe out the nuke threat. Stay tuned.

comments.name: KEVIN C CAIN
comments.body: The uncomfortable reality is that wars like this are not won from 30,000 feet. If the objective is regime change or a decisive military victory, history suggests that it ultimately requires boots on the ground.  No sane American, or even the insane MAGA devotees wants another Iraq or Afghanistan.  The wiser course is to acknowledge that the strategic objectives were unattainable at an acceptable cost, bring the conflict to a close, and redirect our attention to the vulnerabilities it exposed. The United States should be strengthening energy security by rebuilding relationships with reliable partners throughout the Western Hemisphere including Canada, Mexico, Brazil, and, where feasible, Venezuela.  Simultaneously, Trump should launch the equivalent of a new Manhattan Project for advanced energy technologies. The greatest strategic response to oil producing adversaries is not another war it's making their leverage increasingly irrelevant.  If this failed war serves as the catalyst for genuine North American energy independence and technological innovation, it may yet produce one positive legacy.

comments.body: I’m 65. My 88 year old mother is bedridden and my 89 year old father has just been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. I have been taking care of them for the past two years. It’s exhausting, and I’m dealing with the knowledge I’m going to lose them. With babies, you know they’ll grow out of diapers. That isn’t happening with my mom. I’m having to monitor Dad’s meds and make sure he gets enough to eat. The only blessing is that Mom isn’t senile. I love both of them and this just sucks.

comments.name: Mary McNally
comments.body:
My mother was the main caregiver for my dad when he became debilitated by Parkinson’s. My brother and his family lived around the corner from them. He would put Dad to bed every night. My sister-in-law was a godsend. My family is huge but scattered around the country. We all contributed something to the effort. My eldest sister was a registered nurse, so she was the medical advisor. I lived with them for a time, drove them to appointments, and helped them as much as possible around my full-time job. Eventually we hired morning caregivers to assist Dad. Mom had always been a night owl, so that gave her some needed rest. What my brother and I didn’t realize was that she was slipping into dementia. Our siblings noticed it when they visited. 

Ironically Dad’s mind was sharp. He had some hallucinations from the medications he was taking, but he realized he was hallucinating. When it looked like home care was beginning to not be workable and the discussion of assisted living came up, dad asked my mom if she would be going with him. Her response was “no, I’m mobile.” Ironically a couple weeks later she broke her hip and the wheels turned quickly and they were placed together in the same facility. She might have had some event while she had surgery, because afterwards she became frightened and childlike. Being in an unfamiliar environment probably contributed to her fears. They survived only 10 months after the dominoes fell. She passed 40 days after he did.

We waded through 4 inches of slush, (wearing neoprene booties and mitts) and had to push away chunks of ice. We stay in for 5 minutes when it is that cold. SUCH a great feeling, a reset and endorphin rush in a big way. Some of us are very addicted. In winter we go 4-5 times a week. There are several groups of cold water dippers along the coast of Maine. So many northern countries have been doing it for decades. We notice long lasting effects on mood and sleep. And the cameraderie … can’t beat it. Cosmic connection to each other and nature.

I would say our strengths lay in our being a nation of laws with equal protection, a nation of immigrants, and a nation of aspiration. These things were never completely true, but they were true enough that most of us could mostly see ourselves that way. 

But the past few years have tipped us away from that… we have seen laws are only as strong as a president’s ethics, with nothing really there to restrain him and the cronies he protects. Their lawlessness breaks the social contract and begets more lawlessness and less hope. 

We have seen our willingness to reject immigrants and treat them as lawbreakers whether they are or not… and no system can be truly functional if an entire class of people are treated as “less than” … a lesson we should have learned after the civil war, but sadly we did not, so we are no longer attracting the world’s brightest to join us, nor the folks that staff our nursing homes and elder assistance that we desperately need. 

This and the shifting of the national conversation from aspiration to a race to the bottom has all left me struggling to see how we will cope with the urgent challenges of climate change and income inequality. All of which is to say, I am not as hopeful as you, Mr Kristof, but I hope you are right.

However, she has no right to impose either her religious or political beliefs on other young women who wish to choose differently, at least until we are full on Gilead/The Handmaid's Tale.

comments.name: Dana Lawrence
comments.body: Let me guess. Mrs. Waters does not worry about he she will put on the table. She does not worry about health care. She only cares about imposing her beliefs on others, because she has no real worries outside her beliefs. And at 28, she knows so little about how others live, no matter her education. And she does not care.

comments.name: Dorothy
comments.body:
I am in awe of how conservatives in the US can on one side of their mouths, criticize "woke" policies and decry a culture war, while on the other side of their mouths, wage a legal and culture war against women, minorities, LGBTQI and immigrants. 

What is interesting to me in the end, is that neither side of the culture wars are really addressing what is hurting Americans--the obscene power of corporations and the distortion of our economy by these increasingly fewer and fewer corporate entities. We pay over the odds for health care, housing, food and education. No wonder people are in debt, and worried. Culture wars like this one are simply a way to distract from the actual issues at hand. Neither political party are willing to address our structural problems.

comments.name: Orr
comments.body:
She wants to be called Mrs Waters, but a truly traditional name for a married woman would be Mrs Jackson Waters, not Mrs Emma Waters. 
My mother had Mrs "my father's name" on her driver's licence.
(This was in the 1960s.  I know you might think that it's unbelievable, but I have her driving permit in my possession)

Seems that Emma gets to pick and chose which traditions she is adopting.
I'd like to make certain Emma isn't employed specifically to advocate for removing choices for the rest of us women.

comments.name: Richard M
comments.body:
Forget ideology- let's think ecology. There are over eight billion people on this planet. Do we need more? Access to fresh water will be the cause of future wars, after our wars for oil. When I'm stuck on the 405- which is every time- I don't say, gosh, we need more people. I don't say it when I look at the Pacific garbage patch, at the rising sea levels, at the lack of housing. 

And I certainly don't say it when I look at people like Emma Waters, who will create more people who create more people who are oblivious to everything but their own desires.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: I love kids, but barefoot and pregnant is a losing strategy on so many levels. We should be having fewer not more children. We cannot even provide daycare and a good education for the ones we already have. There is no population crises in this country. Don't believe me? Just look at all the would be citizen taxpayers (a.k.a. immigrants) we are turning away and actively deporting.

comments.name: poslug
comments.body:
Well, I might have been able to fit in children if I had extended family but the numbers were wiped out by the flu of 1918 and the diphtheria epidemic after the Civil War plus parental death from tuberculosis (possibly from raw milk but who knows in 1869). 

RFK Jr's anti vaccine campaign never comes up in the Heritage baby farm policy drivers. And raw milk to a toddler? Parental endangerment of a child.

comments.name: Hope
comments.body: How many children one has, the choice to have or not have children, is an intensely personal decision. Not having children is not anti-family, it's a personal choice for that person or couple.  Same with having children.  If Emma wants lots of kids, good for her.  But she shouldn't be telling other women they should make the same choice as she did.

articles.title: A Conservative Role Model for Ending the Fertility Crisis
articles.summary: Emma Waters, pregnant with her third child, is crafting policy to encourage early parenthood. Some think she is pushing an ideology that does not meet reality.

comments.name: Ian
comments.body: I just hope Spain wins the World Cup and look forward to the trophy presentation. Viva Espana!

comments.name: Robert Henry Eller
comments.body:
Trump is the only person who could possibly love Trump.
Anyone else who claims to "like Trump" is working Trump, and working the rest of us.
What seems to be motivating too many humans these days is not flattering. How's the market for mirrors doing? Anyone know?
I'm just finishing Michael Pollan's recent book, "A World Appears," about the (apparently) still wide-open search the understand and explain what humans perceive as "Consciousness."
But looking around, I think humans should pay more attention to understanding and explaining Conscience; it seems to be in short supply.
I cannot name a single demographic I nominally belong to that I belong to. Anyone else? How do you feel about your own "Us"-es? Isn't there something more we can do than just witness what's going on?

comments.name: Eugene O Neill
comments.body: Mr. Trump’s foreign policy of throwing a plate of multinational food at the wall and seeing what sticks has run its course. This is an unmanageable effort because it is precisely designed to be. The President enjoys keeping everyone in his orbit off balance and constantly guessing. His latest NATO hate/love summit in Turkey was yet another example.

comments.name: Philippe
comments.body:
The EU, Canada, and other NATO partners are biding their time, developing military supply lines and expanding their national military industries. These sectors are becoming increasingly interconnected, with the objective of reducing reliance on American military defense infrastructure and industrial capacity.

Trump can continue his self-centered bullying, meanwhile, the adults are busy making alternative plans, bypassing the USA.

comments.name: John Mayflower
comments.body: It's true that the West benefitted from the US's strength and power, but this is at least in part because the US took on the role as de facto leader. It promoted itself as such over decades, both internally and externally; it was not so much that countries "took advantage", more that the US needed to be seen as a provider, benefactor, protector, far-seeing, generous and wise: countries and their leaders responded accordingly. Had it put itself forward as resentful, spiteful, vengeful, petty and capricious, as is now the case, those countries might have made other plans. They are now doing so. I can't imagine any leader having anything other than total contempt for Trump, whether they say it out loud or not.

comments.name: Archibald
comments.body:
The delusion is strong in this one.

One can only imagine what the other national leaders think and say about Trump in private.
How much longer can his enablers in Congress ignore his irrational raging and mercurial volatility?
He is visibly unfit for further service as President. The 25th Amendment is overdue, but ending up with Vance in the job is likely a step too far for many in both parties. 
Perhaps the best strategy is to treat him the way Reagan was protected - move him quickly into  the background and let him sign documents, but keep him out of the media and the public eye as much as possible. By all means stop the late-night rages on X and Truth Social. His Cabinet and WH staff can govern in committee and serve as the public face of the Administration .
Doing so is necessary- he is a real and present danger to the country and the world. He is no longer rational.

comments.name: Jorge
comments.body:
In reporting in so much detail about Trumpian drama and turmoil, 
this story neglects to recite the essential nut graf that readers really deserve to know:  this was a highly successful NATO summit in which the NATO leaders pledged to abide by Article 5, to more fairly fund their collective defense, to pledge tens of billions in new Ukraine funding (and a US promise to transfer Patriot anti-missile tech), and they agreed to collectively reduce dependence on mid-east oil.

Instead all we hear about is Trump "insulting" some Euro leader, and several nameless European leaders gaining a new resolve to go their own way.....

comments.name: Nybol
comments.body:
We are at the point where the insults are either novel or a variation on the same old.  

"Oh, I haven't heard that one before."  The Spanish official then asks his interpreter for any subtle meaning behind the insult, but usually the polyglot shrugs shoulders and says it's gibberish in any language, colleagues nod heads to confirm.  "Well then, let's file this under same old."  Smirks all around...

articles.title: After Insulting Allies at NATO Summit, Trump Says They Love Him
articles.summary: The meeting in Turkey featured President Trump at his most mercurial, veering from scorn to praise for European countries, including some whose patience with mollifying him has worn thin.

comments.name: JJohn
comments.body:
I’m not sure I can muster any compassion for those who follow medical advice from Facebook or sources of information other than a reputable medical professional or websites like The Cleveland Clinic. I’m livid. I have personal reasons for feeling this way. 

Most people do everything right and can still miscarry or lose a child after birth or down the road. It’s devastating. But trying to beat the odds with a baby’s life, when informed at birth of a chance of severe bleeding complications including a horrific death leaves me cold. 

I have a minim amount of compassion for the parents taken in by the quackery abundant online over the quacks. Don’t sue the hospital, work to overturn the protections hosts like Facebook, TwitterX, ect. enjoy from being sued out of existence for allowing this garbage to exist on their platforms. 

We need reforms like the EU, Australia and UK have. Social media content isn’t like a “cork message board” any longer. Opinions are one thing, lies and quackery that goes against proven science shouldn’t be protected. How many kids need to die from no shots or vaccinations before people wake up?

comments.name: A person
comments.body:
How utterly terrifying it would have been to have a child a few hundred years ago, knowing you would likely bury a few babies and small children or have someone bury you. How terrifying that it happens to impoverished or wartorn people around the world even today. 

And how utterly nonsensical that it happens here when parents have the prevention at the ready. I'm astounded at how gruesome this was to read, but I thank you for talking sense.

comments.name: Sylvia HC
comments.body: I gave birth at home, twice, unmedicated and attended by two licensed midwives. In both cases they insisted on the Vitamin K shot after birth. Even in the natural birth community it is known how simple and safe this lifesaving shot really is.

comments.name: Captain Nemo
comments.location: On the Nautilus, Gulf of Texas
comments.body:
If 2.9% of parents refused the shot in 2017 and 5.2% did less than 10 years later, that is not even a doubling.  How then does it make sense that neonatal bleeding was “almost unheard of” in 2017 and no ER doctor had ever seen a case, and now suddenly it’s an epidemic and babies a bleeding left and right?

While I am not disputing the importance of giving Vitamin K perinatally at all (I am a physician myself), I must question the sensational undertone of the article which does not match the statistics.

comments.name: EJ
comments.body:
It is difficult to grasp why anyone would deny a newborn the routine vitamin K injection, which has been the standard of care for over 65 years. Wouldn’t any loving, sensible parent embrace all available interventions to protect their child from life-threatening complications? 

Yet, in recent decades, there has been rising public distrust of the pharmaceutical industry due to its shamelessly profit-driven motives and documented incidents of research misconduct, including outright data manipulation.  

Fundamentally, the solution lies in the pharmaceutical industry’s willingness to regain public trust by prioritizing research transparency, ensuring equitable access to life-saving treatments, and shifting its emphasis to human well-being over shareholder profits.  This would require a complete paradigm shift by the industry toward a nonprofit model. 

As long as the fruits of medical innovation, such as new prescription drugs, vaccines, and targeted therapies, are treated as free-market commodities, this won’t happen.

comments.name: Arthur
comments.body: Parents who refuse this injection violate the most basic of parental responsibility. They are directly responsible for a completely preventable outcome. Parents are supposed to protect their children and as far as I am concerned refusing this injection or vaccines is child abuse.

comments.name: Captain Nemo
comments.location: On the Nautilus, Gulf of Texas
comments.body:
If parents refuse the shot, there is an alternative: Vitamin K can be given orally as an unregulated supplement.  $20 buys enough at Amazon for a dozen babies.  

The catch again is that no specific formulations are “FDA approved”, because naturally oral delivery of the vitamin is less precise than an intramuscular depot injection and there is no control over whether the mother gives it to the baby often enough or not.  So officially these supplements can’t be recommended to these recalcitrant parents as an alternative, because doing so would open the hospital to a malpractice suit if the baby develops a bleed nonetheless.  

So at least part of the problem again is our insanely over-regulated bureaucracy and litigation system, aside from the political polarization.

comments.name: Rick
comments.body: Ideally, this would be an issue where the Director of Health and Human Services could show leadership.

articles.title: As Parents Reject Vitamin K Shots, Some Babies Develop Devastating Bleeding
articles.summary: Doctors described treating brain and abdominal hemorrhages in infants who hadn’t received the routine injection. Several said the images of those patients were seared in their minds.

articles.title: The Intifada at MIT
articles.summary: A professor recounts the experiences of the school’s Jews after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks.

comments.name: Rick C
comments.body:
Racist, Jew-hating Democrats run the universities.

Obviously Sheffi has tenure otherwise he'd be long gone.

comments.name: John Orr
comments.body: How times have changed. If this was the mid-1990s, Jewish Defense League members would have called "batting practice" and put several dozen sidewalk tormenters in the hospital. A few Jewish enforcers could make the progressive latte-shop commandoes think twice before harassing Jewish students and faculty.

comments.name: Chris H
comments.body:
Asked for comment on the book, an MIT spokesman sent a statement pointing out that high percentages of the school’s Jews now say they’re happy and feel safe at the institute.

Night at the Museum: Merenkahre: You are! I love Jews! We owned 40,000 of them!Shepseheret: Such lovely people.Ahkmenrah: Here we go...Larry Daley: They were very happy, always singing with candles...Larry Daley: Yeah. They really weren't happy.Shepseheret: Really?Larry Daley: No, they left. They spent about 40 years in the desert trying to escape.Shepseheret: Oh!

comments.name: Alex Kravtsov
comments.body:
most dispiriting irony: the inverse relationship between the idiocy of student protesters and the prestige of their institutions.

Sooner or later, one or the other will win. An institution cannot remain prestigious for long when some part of it gets increasingly dumb and loud while the other pretends not to notice it.

comments.name: Alan Groff
comments.body:
The girl raised her placard between herself and the student trying to meet her eyes. That image is the whole story.

MIT didn't fail its values. It lived them. The values were already wrong.

The framework calls itself tolerance. Coexist. Every tradition welcome, every symbol honored, every actual claim quietly bracketed in the name of inclusion. It sounds generous. It is totalizing. Having evacuated truth, reason, and history as bases for judgment, it hands decisive power to whoever claims offense most credibly. Not the genuinely wronged — they arrive with particular, irreducible claims that resist the symbol. The framework cannot receive them. It can only receive performances of victimhood in the grammar it has already approved.

So the student seeking eye contact registers as aggressor. The placard-bearer registers as defender. The administration protects the trance and discourages the ones still trying to think.

October 7th happened to particular people. It made particular, unanswerable demands on anyone willing to receive it as real.

The framework raised its placard.

Thomas Mann warned us. The Magic Mountain shows how sensitive people — intelligent, feeling, educated people — get captured by systems that replace encounter with reality with participation in ideology. His insight was precise: the most sensitive individuals feel the failure first. If the institution cannot hear them, the trance doesn't correct.

It deepens.

Sheffi heard them. The question is whether anyone else will.

comments.name: Rob Simard
comments.body:
A Republic cannot survive if its elite institutions teach the next generation that the Republic is illegitimate.

These campus eruptions are not simply spontaneous student protests. They are student outrage weaponized by a professional activist ecosystem: outside agitators, legal-defense networks, nonprofit money, media amplification, and openly anti-American revolutionary politics.

Students are not leading this movement; they are being used by it. They provide the numbers, the optics, and the moral cover. The organizers provide the agenda.

The goal is to delegitimize America’s constitutional order, demoralize young people, and make them ashamed of their own country, the collapse in patriotism among the young is not an accident. It is evidence of intent.

Gallup now finds only 14% of Americans ages 18–34 are “extremely proud” to be American; only 30% are “extremely” or “very” proud. Among all adults, “extremely proud” has fallen from 55% in 2001 to 33% today, and high national pride has dropped from 87% to 53%. This is not just a polling trend. It is the desired outcome of an ideological campaign to convince the next generation that America is illegitimate.

Again - A Republic cannot survive if its elite institutions produce graduates who believe the Republic itself is illegitimate.

comments.name: chris zzz
comments.body: This is not complicated. The progressive woke movement is wickedly against Jews and Israel for many ideological reasons but mainly because they're "settler colonists" and generally code as white/wealthy compared to Gazans. University administrators were either woke and antisemitic  or  too cowardly to stand up to the progressive woke movement's tyrants. With most of them, it's a lot of both.

comments.name: R Kerr
comments.body: The Palestinian agitators harassed Jews in America.  They also wanted Jews out of Israel.  Why did anybody take these conflicting and obnoxious positions seriously?

comments.name: JS
comments.body:
How has Iran over played its hand?  Why did the U.S. have to back down from its aggression?  Because Iran closed down the strait and threatened the world economy with a depression.  That was brilliant.  It can’t match the fire power of our military.  How can Iran possibly give that up when the U.S. and Israel have repeatedly committed aggression against Iran over the years?  How can Iran compel the U.S. to give back its stolen bank reserves and remove our illegal, unauthorized sanctions (war crimes)?  How can Iran give that up when oral commitments and signed treaties by the U.S. are worthless.  Let’s look only at Iran.  The U.S. unilaterally pulled out of the JCPOA (in writing) which Iran was adhering to.  Kushner and Witkoff went to Iran twice for negotiations and it was a ruse to prepare for aggression twice.

It was the U.S. that committed aggression.  How can Iran’s response be unreasonable?  Which of Iran’s demands are unreasonable?  We lost the war.  What concessions did Japan and Germany get after WW II?
The U.S. is not going to pay reparations. So, Iran will charge fees just like Turkey charges fees in the Bosporus Straits.  Look at all the countries we bomb- none of them are compensated and the U.S. is not  held accountable.

comments.name: Hamilton Federalist
comments.body:
What hand is being "overplayed?"  The simple fact ignored by nearly all is the US Navy cannot sail the entire length of the Gulf of Hormuz for fear of being sunk, by Iran's air and sea drones or missiles.  The Taliban defeated the US in Afghanistan and the never possessed airpower, tanks nor drones.  Iran possesses the cards. Trump doesn't have enough troops to keep and hold any Iranian territory.  

Trump is already lying that Iran is desperate to cut a deal but the facts in the Gulf of Hormuz say otherwise.  Label this Iran's second defeat of Trump. Besides Trump knows oil runs out in August so Trhmp will do his TACO dance and declare "victory."

comments.name: Roger
comments.body: This is a very short term view of the situation, Iranians don't think in terms of weeks, days, months, but are weighing this conflicts impact on their country over the next decade. They view this as a very lucrative opportunity and know Western aligned countries are depleting military assets and oil reserves alarmingly fast. Every intercepted drone and missile, everyday the strait remains closed makes Iran stronger, the West aligned nations in an inferior position. It's actually kind of genius

comments.name: Bill
comments.body: Current wars and history tell us bombing alone does not win wars against determined opponents.  Wars are won by foot soldiers.  Ukraine now and in living memory Viet Nam, Japan and Germany are examples.

comments.name: Benny Profane
comments.body: I am not sure which country is overplaying its hand. Iran endured  8 years of war from 1980 until 1988 after being attacked by Iraq under Saddam Hussein. The Iranian regime is willing to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of its citizens, including children, and in general will not hesitate to make the whole population suffer. I think the U.S. leadership and media are again grossly under-estimating Iran's capacity to survive under adverse conditions. And I wish so much they were wrong.

comments.name: Benign Curmudgeon
comments.body: Amusing. Iran doesn’t seem to be risking much of anything. They play with Trump like a dog plays with a chew toy. They don’t respect him and they don’t fear him. And why shouid they?

comments.name: Howard Lightning
comments.body: I fail to see how Iran is “overplaying their hand.” Iran controls the Strait despite repeated US attacks. Trump foolishly miscalculated when he started this illegal war. It is Trump and his incompetent administration who overplayed their hand. Nothing will stop Iran from blocking the Strait and affecting world oil prices anytime they want. That’s the lesson Trump has taught them.

comments.name: toom
comments.body: Situation unclear. Trump and Bibi attack Iran, kill leaders and many others, and after lots of talk, Iran starts up a war again. To me, it sounds like Iran is hoping to influence the midterms and limit Trump as never before. Correct me if I am wrong.

articles.title: Tanker Attacks Risk Overplaying Iran’s Hand and Reigniting a War
articles.summary: Iran’s history shows it is willing to dig in, even when it may suffer big losses.

comments.name: Chris C.
comments.body:
Paris works just fine . . . a couple of minutes, tops. If I'd missed a flight, though, I'd be hopping mad.

The key thing, though, is that it wasn't clear to me or other passengers that our biometrics were being collected and kept. Seems like a lot to ask for a visitor who is only going there to spend thousands of dollars on their economy.

comments.name: JOHN
comments.body: Why would the European Commission listen to people's appeals, esp. people who make money?  Once the EU elite decides something should be done, something like productivity or economic feasibility or public convenience will not stop the illuminati from their vision.  Just like air conditioning: Queen Ursula decreed it be turned off for the lower floors but kept on for the unelected commissars on the uppers that make policy.  The faster the EU disappears, the better European peoples will be.

comments.name: Laust
comments.body: The problem is not Europe, the problem is that your countries does not have biometric data in your pasports.

comments.name: Ray
comments.body:
Bumpy rollouts are expected for any government led program. The private sector would have field tested the technology and protocols with enough time to make adjustments prior to a continent wide deployment.  Bureaucracrats don't work that way.  Suffer the customer while they fix the mess they made. (PS - the surge of US flights was troublesome long before these terminals were introduced)

While Europe has every right (and obligation) to protect its borders, it seems to me that this was a rushed 'tit for tat' response to the very similar system run by the US DHS which has had few complaints. The EU wants to show the world it can go toe to toe with its US "partner" (now frenemy). Yet in critical areas it doesn't seem to have the chops. Tough medicine.  The continent is fragmented and as a result, the EU is ailing.

Mario Draghi is right. The EU does not have unlimited time to leverage this moment to get itself together.  What Draghi didn't say, but I will is this: it would be much easier to do it WITH THE US as a partner.

comments.name: Lawrence Ginsberg
comments.body: FRA is a true nightmare consequent to this policy. I lost considerable time there recently and I'm sure flights are being missed.

comments.name: Mmm
comments.body: I thought the EU just hated the UK after Brexit, but it seems they hate everybody.

comments.name: Jane
comments.body: We went through the EES lines in Barcelona in late April.  I was dreading the multi-hour waits I’d read about.  It was a little confusing, but we were  through the lines and out of the airport in literally 20 minutes.

comments.name: rbitset
comments.body:
My recent experience is that the airlines are doing nothing to help mitigate the problems. I flew two weeks ago to Munich on United Airlines. There was no mention before the flight or on the flight about the details of the new border security. A single sheet of paper that clearly spelled out the process would have greatly sped up getting through border control.

Similarly, Lufthansa didn’t provide any information about the border control procedures on my departure.

I have had business travel to Europe several times a year for the last decade so am pretty comfortable with the Munich airport. But after this trip, I’m still not totally sure what the process is supposed to be.

articles.title: Europe’s New Entry/Exit System Is a Mess, and It’s Not Going Away
articles.summary: E.U. leaders rebuffed a plea from the aviation industry to pause the biometric checkpoints, which have caused long lines and missed flights. Summer travelers beware.

comments.name: Phil Glau
comments.body:
Bury the lede twice in this article:

(1) about the same number of violations of other inspections firms. 

(2) Fine for violation only $1000 

Given the low cost of getting caught and that all the other inspection firms have about the same number of recorded violations points the finger at NYC, not this particular inspection firm. Sure, perhaps they did sloppy work on this job, but it seems like any firm that had been hired instead would likely have done about the same caliber work because the city has abdicated code enforcement to private companies which are highly incentivized to 'please the customer' because the fines for getting caught doing so are low.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body: There are no words, except corruption, which seems to be a great, great thing these days.    Until it fails....

comments.name: Seal Team Sith
comments.body: Whoever did the structural engineering analysis should be out of a job.  They are incompetent and could have caused the injury and death of many people.  How they could have been so wrong with their engineering is impossible to understand.  They approved the addition of floors above an existing structure and totally missed that the existing structure could not take the load.  Yes, the city inspector should have caught it, but whoever did the initial structural engineering analysis is most at fault.

comments.name: JBT
comments.body: The inspector may have missed the problems, but somebody designed that building and someone built it!  Why focus on the last guy in the chain?

comments.name: Margaret Healey
comments.body: Hmmm. Kind of makes you understand how amazing NYC is when so many details are done right.  You can blame the inspector for missing something or you can blame the architect, construction firm etc.  but it feels almost inevitable in the times when expertise is not respected and everything else seems corrupt.  The real result of trickle-down philosophy.

comments.name: Maxxmanx
comments.body: I think they're going to have a hard time selling these units after this.

comments.name: HarryB
comments.body: Who is going to want to live in that building even if it is ever finished? Imagine the sales pitch: the famous building that almost collapsed and you can live there!

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:
The inspector was probably paid by the builders to 'ignore' these issues. 
There are few, if any, businesses more corrupt than the construction business in New York. A perfect example is Trump. He grew up in that business and learned all the lessons well.

articles.title: Inspector of Buckling Building Cited for Missing Problems at Other Sites
articles.byline: Stefanos Chen, Dionne Searcey, Asmaa Elkeurti and Mihir Zaveri
articles.summary: A New York Times review of city records shows that the firm, Domani Inspection Services, was repeatedly accused of breaking New York City rules.

articles.title: Socialists Spell Trouble for Democrats
articles.summary: They can win in deep-blue districts, but they’ll weigh down the party elsewhere.

comments.name: Marion Anderson
comments.body: Colorado has been taken over by Democrats for the past two decades.  We were once a moderate Republican oriented state.  Not any longer.  The Democratic Socialists of America want to run our lives and take our money while imposing their will.  The 'hate' expressed by the DSA for our country is appalling and I hope the country wakes up to the reality of what some wish for.

comments.name: Bruce Fernandes
comments.body:
Trump trying to use government resources to save the coal industry.  Picking losers and using government policy to make a winner that markets have determined are losers.

Trump using government resources to take interests in businesses he and only he decides are strategically important.

That's one part of socialist policies.

comments.name: Mary Ellen Higgins
comments.body: There wouldn't be so many socialist candidates if capitalism hadn't been allowed to run amok. The spoils of our capitalist economy are going largely to the rich. The already rich are getting much much richer while the poor struggle. The wealthy should be taxed at higher rates to bring down the deficit. We need universal health care because many people are uninsured and Trump did not continue the generous additions to Medicaid that Biden passed. The people reading WSJ have no idea how hard it is to live on $12 per hour. In Pennsylvania, the minimum wage is still $7.25 per hour.

comments.name: Yuri Feldman
comments.body: Rove is correct that Socialists can win in select urban districts which do not understand economics or in select small states with small populations (like Vermont), but have no chance in broader America, or even in states with a population greater than 1 million.  Socialism is fundamentally anti-American, which goes against our culture of innovation and entrepreneurship.

comments.name: Frank Groff
comments.body: sorry karl, but throwing out words like "socialism" and "communism" to scare ordinary americans from voting against their own best interests isn't working any more.  in a day and age when musk has reached trillionaire status, the ellisons are snatching up media companies like I collect stamps and the uber wealthy are writing off their private jets while teachers are paying for school supplies out of their own pocket, your pearl clutching, fear-mongering words ring hollow.  many americans are one health crisis away from living in their cars, a trip to the grocery store requires a payday loan, filling up the tank leads to sticker shock, student loan debt is lifelong debt and the GOP are now threatening to cut or even eliminate social security.  for what?  so that the richest among us can get even richer??  FORGET IT!  the most productive and happiest countries in the world don't have the preposterous wealth gap that the USA does.  what they share in common is a strong social safety net.  we can do better.

comments.name: Scott P
comments.body: Wait a minute Karl. I thought Trump won in a landslide in the last election that gave him carte blanche to herd up immigrants like cattle? You're admitting it was a razor close election? That might hinder your ability to get any inside info from the White House in the future. Just don't make the fatal mistake of saying the 2020 election wasn't rigged and that Joe Biden really won.

comments.name: KEN M
comments.body: Do colleges screen persons who want to be a "doctoral candidate" for knowledge of civics, common sense?  Might they ask questions that an eight grader could answer such as: are police departments and prisons necessary for society, should a nation have and protect its borders, etc?

comments.name: Jeff Lewis
comments.body: Socialism destroys ambition.

comments.name: Leonard George
comments.body: The world is changing fast, a time of danger and promise. Canada, led by the astute PM Carney, is helping to create a new world that could be better than the old order. I wish my American neighbours the very best as they figure out how to join this project. comments.name: Civil Disobedience
comments.body:
The biggest issue I see with the idea of colonizing Mars is that most people already struggle to live in the harshest regions of Earth. Places like Alaska, Siberia, Antarctica, and other polar environments push people, and these are still on our home planet. They have breathable air, familiar gravity, natural landscapes, weather, animals, plants, rivers, mountains, and all the other things human beings evolved alongside.

Even then, strange things happen to people during long, cold winters with little sunlight. People become restless, depressed, irritable, or desperate for a change. In Alaska, plenty of people leave multiple times a year just to get sunlight, see family, or remember what the rest of the world feels like. So how would this work on Mars?

On Mars, there would be no forest to walk into, no ocean to stand beside, no town to drive to, no weekend escape, and no simple way home. Every room, hallway, and living space would remind you that you were surviving inside a machine. And what happens when someone starts to feel trapped? You would not simply be isolated in a remote place. You would be isolated on another planet, months or years from Earth, with no real possibility of relief.

The question, then, is not just whether we can build rockets powerful enough to reach Mars. It is about whether human beings can psychologically endure a life in which nearly every basic experience has to be mediated by technology.

Like sports betting, the ease of "investment" totally hidden from the criticism of wiser judgement is just between the gambler and his cellphone until he loses big. As AI companies moderate their ranting to suggest they'll bring an employment revolution benefitting all mankind they have laid off over 100,000 workers because... AI.

comments.name: Skip Wenz
comments.body:
"Me." "I." 

Chatbot interactions with humans are phony. If you ask Gemini a question, it will give you an answer and then ask, "Would you like 'me' to tell you more about X?" There is no "me." The LLMs are nothing but collections of programs running on collections of silicon chips. The people who program this nonsense either want to seem user friendly to make humans feel more comfortable using their technology (and make more money), or have cynically decided to seduce the gullible into thinking they are "talking" to a "friend" to control their minds. Witness AI "therapists." 

The proper question isn't "would you like me to tell you more?", but would you like to learn more? (Or "like more information about?")

comments.body: Irony died when AI giants started complaining about “intellectual property theft”

comments.name: John

comments.name: V

US AI companies will bite the dust, scraping for the bits of the super premium segment, while 95% of tokens flow to Chinese AI. AI investors will be left holding the baby and the bathwater.

articles.title: Did We Make the Wrong Bet on Big A.I.?
articles.summary: Maybe Anthropic and OpenAI are not the future of artificial intelligence.

comments.name: Cara
comments.body: Re snapping wife — I agree, keep this about her effect on you. Many many wives have shouldered the burden of decades of responsibility for remembering, organizing, doing all the things that make the couple’s life function. Snapping is a terrible way to deal with conflict, and she especially shouldn’t be doing this in front of guests/friends. But there may have 30 years of neglect, obliviousness, and aggravation behind those sharp comments. So it’s best not to give advice to the wife on how to interact with her husband. We just don’t know what happens in other’s relationships.

comments.name: rai
comments.body:
My dog is very elderly. She is happy and still enjoys life for now.
But yes, shes not as sleek and beautiful as she was 17 years ago. She has small lipomas and seed sized benign fiberous tumors all over, missing many teeth. Her fur is patchy and grey, her eyes are cloudy and shes a bit stiff from arthritis.

But shes been my constant companion for over a decade and a half. Shes been under vet care and I dont care how much it costs to keep her quality of life up. Once she stops enjoying life and lets me know its time to go, I wont keep her here for my selfishness. But until then, I will do whatever it takes to keep her comfortable and happy. Regardless of if she is aesthetically pleasing to anyone else.

comments.name: Rick
comments.body: Some people lose the filter and become much more critical of their spouse as they age. It’s a big reason for gray divorce. My uncle divorced his wife of 30 years because she was unable to control her endless negativity.

comments.name: Kris R
comments.body:
My sister and I live on different coasts. We are 13 months apart and are dear friends. I only see her once or twice a year. One time I was going to visit her and we had plans to go to a B&B on the Chesapeake. Her daughter invited herself and of course it changed the whole trip.

When my sister was coming to my coast for our son’s very small wedding, the same daughter, who was 35! invited herself to the wedding. My son and DIL were very gracious but it shocks me how selfish the daughter is and how clueless my sister is. Of course my sister watches the daughter’s year old son for 2 days a week. The other 2 grandparents watch him the other 3 days. They are all over 70 and the daughter is an attorney. Just boggles my mind.

comments.name: JOR
comments.body: Regarding the wife who snaps at her husband during a get-together with friends, I think the LW should not address this at all with the wife in question. This couple's relationship and interactions, although in public, are not the business of others. Either keep politely silent or stop socializing with this couple. But commenting on the wife's behavior is intrusive and not acceptable.

comments.name: Andy
comments.body:
Usually I agree with Philip and differ only on minor details, but not this time. LW1 If you had kept the dinner a secret from the Mom she would have been more angry than she is now and wouldn't trust you in the future. I think you did the best you could in a hard situation. You set your limits and were willing to deal with the other persons disappointment. Just make sure that you tell your niece about it so she's not surprised when her mother complaines to her about being excluded (I have a hunch the niece is used to it...)

LW2 Before you call out the wife saying that you don't like what she is doing, ask her husband if he want's you to talk to her about it. He might have other ideas about how to handle things than you do. Once you dress down the wife, especially if the husband is there, you're likely to see a lot less of them and it sounds like the husband can use all the friends he can get.

comments.name: KC
comments.body:
L1 might be a sibling jealousy or territorial thing between mom and grown sister 

Have a sister with two daughters. We all live on the same city. One daughter invited me over for lunch  while home on maternity leave when I got there her mother (my sister) “dropped in “ and proceeded to make snarky comments about my one child’s sexuality preference. Just ignored it and chalked it up to her insecurity. 
Happened again when mom took off work to come downtown to another lunch with other daughter that was a standing date daughter had set up when our work schedules coincided  same snarky comments. 
Silver lining-
Has helped me be aware and kind when my sibs meet up with my adult children on their own

comments.name: Grant
comments.body:
Yea I just had a similar issue with my daughter around some plans that we have, where I first asked her if it would be cool if another family member might join, but she preferred not, so I didn’t ask. 

But no harm in asking, maybe she would have liked that.

And sure, it might be awkward when we head out without them, and if they ask to come along, more awkward, and if they’re offended about not being asked to come along, more awkward still.

And then we’ll move on. 

Personally that didn’t seem to need to be a whole drama thing of a referendum on everyone’s relationships and psychology and how if so and so didn’t do what I think they should have done then it’s their fault that I’m feeling awkward about it.

But then we are commenting on the social q’s column, so maybe drama is our thing.

Democracy is a framework that enables us all to exercise that freedom, limited only by our respect for others to exercise their freedoms.  These freedoms are embodied in rights, which allow us to exercise our rights to the extent that they do not interfere with the rights of others.

comments.name: Timothy Smith

articles.byline: Ryan Felton | Photography by Jintak Han for WSJ
articles.summary: After 10 deaths, regulators are warning the public about air bags in used cars with components marked as made by a Chinese company, but tracing them is difficult.

comments.name: doug carlisle

comments.name: Prashant J

So he couldn't legally license it south of the border, even with a retrofitted (by BMW) airbag. I guess this is the reason why--they couldn't be certain of the quality/reliability of the airbag in meeting federal requirements.

comments.name: Alan Rose
comments.body:
10 deaths, versus thousands of others saved. 

Regrettable, but hardly a mass tragedy.

comments.name: I Stephens
comments.body: Carfax is notoriously unreliable in its records, counting on voluntary reporting of events.  There is a great likelihood that the individuals like those making the repairs in this article would not report their activities to anyone. Why divulge information that reduces the value of the vehicle you want to sell?

comments.name: petey b
comments.body: Why does a genuine air bag cost $1000 as implied in the article?  Maybe if the genuine thing didn't cost so much there wouldn't be a thriving market in fakes.

Well, the federal govt. mandated that those bombs be in cars for decades. Maybe some thinking about that should be considered.

comments.name: Gerald Krug
comments.body: Why not allow owners to disable the airbags? Instead, hook the starter to the driver's seat belt, so the vehicle won't start until clicked. Finally, if the occupants are not wearing seat belts, there should be no liability for injuries assigned to the other driver even if at-fault.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: I don't disagree with the idea that Canada and Europe should do much more in the way of their own defense . . . and as witnessed by the actions of our Prime Minister Canada is. . . . so the US strategy on this makes great sense . . .  their tactics to do so very much do not in my mind. The outcome given how this is playing out will be a Canada and Europe who by strenthening themselves less likely to see the need to engage with the US in ways that I am sure the US would like to see happen . . . and in our case we are becoming a country that sees the US as purely a transactional relationship where if it makes sense for both parties for something to happen . . . it will . . . other than that the US is fast becoming for many of us I suspect a flyover country . . .  it did not have to be this way . . . but when someone of that character is elected and is someone who sees everything as a nail so only a hammer is needed that is what you get . . .

comments.name: chambolle
comments.body:
At this point, I’m not sure why European nations would not consider U.S. military bases located within their sovereign territories as a hostile occupation force. The U.S. has no more right to maintain military  bases in Germany and Spain than Germany and Italy have the right to maintain bases in Maine and North Carolina. They’re doing us a favor; they don’t have to continue doing it.

And in case no one remembers, it wasn’t all that long ago the U.S. did not want Italy and Germany to arm themselves, for reasons apparent to anyone able to recall the minor matter of those two World Wars. We built our bases there as an occupation force, not out of the goodness of our hearts.

Why wouldn’t the EU nations just bulk up their own military manufacturing, which they’re perfectly capable of doing; grow their economies on weapons production, as we’ve done ever since we entered WW II; and then advise the U.S. to pack its bags and leave.

There’s only one way to deal with a bully, especially a cowardly bully like Donald Trump: punch him right in the nose — something I learned as a puny, bullied kid. Nine times out of ten, the bullies just run home screaming for their Mom.

I cannot wait for the day when the response to Trumps bluster is: show us your plans to remove US presence from our countries and keep in mind the consequences…

comments.name: JSK
comments.body: Whenever this much money is vested in a few companies (i.e. control of pharmaceutical insurance) there are going to be serious problems. Letting these industries self-police is an ongoing and horrible mistake. While a national policy makes sense, any state efforts could serve as a future model to help control abuses. One big area that needs to be fixed: pre-authorization policies for many new medications where these large pharmaceutical insurers restrict access. But some of these hopes for future improvements will also require better and simultaneous control of another massively wealthy industry: big pharma.

comments.name: DesertMD
comments.body:
“We owe it to our patients to do everything in our power to stop these misguided laws from taking effect,” said Susan Peppers, an executive overseeing Express Scripts.

Express Scripts provides a horrible patient experience. I coordinate my elderly father's healthcare and dealing with them is a nightmare of delays, poor communication, and lengthy prior authorization processes. Ms Peppers - we owe it to patients to regulate the vital delivery of medications to our older and vulnerable folks and eliminate parasitic PBMs from the system.

comments.name: sandra M
comments.body: Something needs to be done.  The states would likely have huge support about breaking these huge companies apart.  Outside this issue, I've seen this past year insurance companies mandating that patients change their treatment for immune deficiency.  It's extremely expensive for sure in the 5 figures.  There are different brands and choices whether to spread a dose out weekly or monthly.  The product is either infused with a pump into subcutaneous tissue weekly or through an IV monthly.  While many products/brands are alike there can be specific features about a product where the patient has a much lower chance of having a significant drug reaction. Reactions are actually pretty common and it may take a patient months to find the right product/brand that they do well on.  Now all of a sudden, these insurance companies are taking choices away.  Both the brand of product and whether it's weekly or monthly.  I'm stunned that insurance companies have the capability of forcing their patients to do this.  This year has been far worse than any years prior.  The whole business of insurance has just been a mess.  We should not have for-profit medicine.

comments.name: marylee

comments.name: Heiko Muhr

Putin appeaser Trump has not supported the Ukrainian struggle. European and Canadian support dwarfs what our great country provided in 2025 and 2026. comments.name: KDL
comments.body: What about the disconnection from nature? The loss of a sense of deep human interdependence with nature in modern life is THE culprit, it could be argued. A sense of the divine and transcendent certainly can come from a recognition of the reality that we are just one part of creation and are mutually responsible for the thriving of other living things. Perhaps these Christians don’t want to go there because they have to read the Bible literally and some writer, years ago, wrote of man’s dominion. That, indeed, may be the real original sin. Until humans reconcile, with humility, that they are a critical, yes, but also expendable part of creation and that a sense of purpose exists in learning how to work in concert with other living things to sustain ourselves and, since MrDouthat seems to love and need a good maximizing project, maximize the bounty and beauty of nature itself through right relationship with all living things . . . Until that happens life will indeed likely be experienced as less meaningful. I notice indigenous peoples who have a semblance of self-determination have no issues with finding life a miracle and locating purpose, with or without attachment to a monotheistic practice. They don’t need to dominate to feel alive. They never lost their understanding and practice of relationality with other living beings. It’s enough.

comments.name: GustofWind
comments.body: These guys can't let go of their old, outdated, obsolete stories.  They don't want to move on, though, because they think that secularists and humanists cannot create meaning and purpose in their lives. That may be true for most of our public because they have not put the work in to imagine, author and enact a new narrative to provide meaning in their lives. But I'm a Naturalist, and feel fully capable of creating my own meaning and purpose in life.  What is it with people who keep reaching back for a past that doesn't exist anymore? Why can't they move on to create meaning through new stories and narratives that we author and enact in our lives today? Today! I don't want to live by ancient stories the author and his guest wish to REenact, because they lack the imagination to create something anew. Douthat and Dreher are stuck in the past. Let's leave them there!

comments.name: Al
comments.body: The op-ed’s opposition to modernity falls directly into the trap warned against in Ecclesiastes 7:10, which counsels that it is not wise to ask why the old days were better. Romanticizing the past relies on a distorted memory that ignores historical hardships, while unfairly criticizing the progress of our current era. Solomon reminds us in Ecclesiastes 7:14 that God creates both good times and bad times, meaning every era has its unique blessings and burdens. Rejecting the modern world means dismissing the tools and advancements we have been given to steward, falsely suggesting that God was more capable or present in the past than He is today.True biblical wisdom requires us to engage faithfully with the reality of the present rather than escaping into an idealized version of yesterday. Fixating on an imagined golden age breeds paralysis and discontentment, which stops us from doing the good work required of us right now. Instead of wishing for a different time, Ecclesiastes 7:11-12 emphasizes that wisdom acts as a preservation and a shelter in the face of life's uncertainties. By embracing the present with gratitude and adaptability, we honor divine providence and focus our energy on building a meaningful future rather than longing for a past that never truly existed.

comments.name: JP
comments.body:
If the concern is that people need a sense of purpose in their lives, I do not think supporting Trump is the way to give it to them.

People often find purpose by believing their work helps others. They want a place to belong. They want to feel that they are contributing to a community that recognizes and values them.
A teacher feels purpose when she believes she is helping her students. A public defender feels purpose when he believes he is helping vulnerable people. That sense of contribution—of helping one’s community and taking pride in that work—is one thing that gives life meaning.

So how do we cultivate it? By building communities where people do not feel exploited or disposable. By paying a living wage. By refusing to make people work understaffed. By preventing less moral actors from outcompeting decent people through cruelty, corruption, or abuse.

Politically, that means rejecting the politics Trump represents. A politics built on domination, resentment, and exploitation does not give people real purpose. It gives them enemies.

On the governmental side, it means using regulation to restrain immoral business practices that create unfair advantages. As Weber recognized, modern society depends on people who handle other people’s money, rights, and interests. So when immoral conduct becomes profitable, even decent actors are pressured to adopt it.

We got minimum wage because people wanted to help workers out, not because of benevolence of the market or employers.

comments.name: Dr. Tim Radak
comments.body: There’s also another reason to be cautious in usage of Omega-3 supplements, particularly at high doses, such as from what the recent Yassine, 2026 study you mentioned used ie 2g DHA: atrial fibrillation. A meta-analysis of seven trials with long term use of Omega 3 fish oil supplements suggested an increase risk of atrial fibrillation and at doses much less than the what the Yassine study used, with increasing doses further increasing risk (Gencer, 2021). Another study (UK Biobank) also confirmed this in healthy populations with no cardiovascular disease in which regular use of fish oil supplements resulting in no primary prevention benefit and instead, an increased risk for atrial fibrillation and also stroke (Chen, 2024).  The American Heart Association highlights the heart-brain axis in their Scientific Statement that atrial fibrillation may compromise cerebral blood flow potentially damaging small blood vessels in the brain and creating microhemorrhages instrumental to cognitive function (Testai, 2024). A meta-analysis suggested a twice-fold increase risk for dementia in those with atrial fibrillation (Kwok, 2011) while another suggested a 1.4 to 2.2 fold increase risk for dementia or cognitive impairment (Koh, 2022; Papanastasiou, 2021).

I’m the founder of a reading platform built around this exact problem, so I’m admittedly biased — but I don’t think the answer is to simplify Homer or replace the poem with a summary. The better challenge is helping readers stay with the original text while recovering enough context to keep going.

In Swedish it's titled STRÄNDERNAS SVALL, which would translate as something like "shores' swell." I recommend trying to track it down if you're a committed Odysseyophile.

comments.name: Kb
comments.body:
Sazan should be environmentally restored and serve as nature preserve, much like Lokrum Island near Dubrovnik. 
While visiting Croatia recently I noticed the look of wonder on my daughter’s faces when they saw Plitvice, the red cliffs, the blue of the Adriatic Sea, the untouched beauty of the country. In those moments I could feel their joy and emotion, their sense of wholeness. It made me think about the situation in Albania. Albanians have a right to the beauty of their country. All humans need to be in nature to feel whole, it’s a human right and it connects us all. The countries along the Adriatic are truly stunning and the people who live there have a right to enjoy its true beauty. Tourists can visit but it belongs to them - it’s not a private island. The thought of a golf course and casino destroying that gorgeous land makes my heart ache. I hope the project is halted and nature prevails. Flamingos fight on!

It is strangely fortunate that the poison of past regimes has thus far prevented the "development" of Sazan, putting it into a position where it is spoiled only by land mines and asbestos dumps, rather than luxury hotels and upscale shops. How ironic that the former circumstances result in a landscape that is more pristine.

If the government and people of Albania have any sense at all, they will have an "Italian strike" over any prospective investments proposed by anyone associated with the foul name Trump. Turn instead to the EU for assistance cleaning up and preserving this gem, without the despicable corrupt amerikan billionaires.

comments.body: This is really bad news in my opinion. Football should be played outdoors. The weather and particularly the cold is an interesting variable and part of the tradition. I love old school cold weather teams like the Packers, Bears and Bills. I can’t stand teams that play in domes, or even in warm climates like Florida or Arizona. This is a disturbing trend, another example of the focus on physical and monetary comfort taking away a traditional part of life that makes it worth living. comments.name: FromBK2LA
comments.body:
One of the most troubling parts of modern messaging is how quickly an accusation becomes a public conviction. Headlines explode, reputations are destroyed, and readers rush to judgment long before any investigation or trial has taken place.

Then, just as quickly, the story often disappears. If the accused drops out or fades from public life, many of these cases never seem to result in charges or a trial, and the the public are rarely left with any explanation of what became of them. Why? What happened to the media's and reader's original passion for accountability? 

That doesn't mean accusations should be dismissed from the start. Serious claims deserve to be investigated thoroughly, and genuine victims deserve to be heard. But due process should matter. Allegations should be the beginning of a search for the truth, not the end of it. A society that treats accusations as proof of guilt should concern everyone, regardless of politics or personal moral standing.

Employers no longer want to train newly minted grads, so obtaining internships is essential from Day 1. The colleges need to do more to educate their students about this and to create partnerships in the business world so that placements can be made. Students need to learn to use their school's career development services and not wait until their senior year. Unfortunately, most do not until it is too late. And students and recent grads need to learn how to network and seek mentors and advocates. Uploading a resume and pushing send on LinkedIn is not a job search. They need to learn to go the extra step - e.g., find grads of your school who work in the fields and at companies of interest. Message them on LinkedIn. Email them. Ask for time just to discuss their own jobs and career path. People like talking about themselves and a good many will want to help. I know first hand that that's how my own daughter got her first job. A complete stranger got her in the door for an initial screening and then she did the rest. Otherwise, no job. comments.body:
Donald J. Trump’s greatest political legacy may not be any single policy, but the model of power he has demonstrated. Around the democratic world, ambitious political leaders are watching what can be achieved by attacking institutions, demanding personal loyalty, and testing constitutional limits.

We continue to describe such movements as “far left” or “far right,” yet those labels increasingly obscure what they have in common. Rather than true opposites, the political extremes often resemble the Yin and Yang of modern politics—each defining itself against the other, each dependent on the other’s existence, and each ultimately pursuing the same objective: the concentration of power.

The real warning is not Donald Trump himself. It is the possibility that he has helped normalize a political template that others, whatever their ideology, will be tempted to emulate.

Have we so intellectually impoverished ourselves that we cannot imagine a story about our history from scratch, without cannibalizing a popular best-seller?

Read Hamlin Garland's stories about pioneer farming

comments.body:
Some readers wonder why Le Pen is running for the 4th time when she has failed 3 times already. 

French politics work differently than the American version.

In France it is not unheard of to run and fail a couple of times before being elected President. Mitterrand was elected President on the *third* try (1965, 1974, 1981). Chirac as well (1981, 1988, 1995). They both went on to win reelection (Mitterrand in 1988 and Chirac in 2002). 

Legal problems aside, there is nothing strange about Le Pen running again. Especially since her party has gone from a fringe phenomenon to now being the most popular in France. Marine Le Pen herself has seen her score go up with every try: in 2012 she got 18% in the first round and was eliminated; in 2017 she got 21% in the first round and went on to get 34% in the second round; in 2022 she got 23% in the first round and 41.5% in the second round.  

Given this linear progression, her huge popularity, and historical precedent, she has every reason to believe she can clutch victory this time. Which obviously doesn't mean she will, but in her universe it makes sense to try again.

comments.name: Not_today
comments.body: This was me throughout my entire youth. My friends called my fixations "death-crushes." My face would flush when he, whoever he was, walked in the door; my stomach would drop. I'd often become friends with him in an effort just to be around and see if anything would happen. Meanwhile, anyone who clearly had a crush on me - usually a nonzero number - was too needy, too forward, too... something. Not what I wanted. It was a painful way to be. At the time I felt I was a 'defective' girl. My mother, seeing how much I couldn't stop myself from calling whatever boy I liked, told me to 'sit on my hands.' Friends told me I didn't think, act, date 'like a girl.' I couldn't sit and wait to be chosen, or give an interested party a chance. I had to chase. I used to say it felt like being pushed by an unseen hand. I broke out of it in my early 20s by finally seeing things through with one of my on-again-off-again targets, who contacted me again after some years and he pursued renewing the connection. We had a brief affair and I just let my heart (or pride?) be broken, got mad at him for being evasive, and got over it. It freed me to stop wondering what might be, and consider/try other kinds of relationship dynamics, having finally learned that feeling obsessed wasn't going to lead to the kind of connection you can sustain for a year or 20. I have been married over 20 years now. When I was diagnosed neurodivergent as an adult, it made more sense.

comments.name: RobS
comments.body: One of the biggest faults of NAGPRA is the guilty before proven innocent approach to finding the right tribe to contact for every item that may or may not be illegally received - not just human remains.  In most cases, finding the authorized designee of the 575 tribes who can verify, resolve, approve, and receive items is next to impossible.  Many tribes simply vanished, leaving no one to verify the approval of ownership.  Museums are having to devote large numbers of staff and interns just for provenance research and repatriation.  Many museums around the country have had to close much of their native collections to the public, whether by removing them from cases into storage or placing brown paper over entire exhibition cases - sometimes almost all of the collections are shielded from view.  Anything from bowls, clothing, jewelry, personal items, textiles, and, yes, human remains, have to have scholar-level provenance research and tribal approval before going back on view.  A Herculean task which is appropriate and necessary, but very difficult to do.

Even major businesses in China must have representatives from the CCP in their leadership once they reach a certain size or influence. This is a key difference between communist and authoritarian dictatorships. The latter can be very brutal, but they generally tolerate other institutional centers of influence. Totalitarian regimes like China’s, however, have learned from the cautionary tale of Poland, where the Catholic Church and trade unions were allowed enough autonomy to become a fatal threat to the Communist regime.

It's a complex engineering system, with precise servos, controllers, sensors, and a control system that dates back to the 90s with software that has been modified by hundreds of people.  All the nuance from lessons learned and institutional knowledge has to be rebuilt.  Some of the exquisite components include a cast silica cap for the radome, a hydraulic system to control the fins, solid fuel pulse motors for terminal attitude control, and a traveling wave tube for the radar.   The missile has been through decades of testing and trials, so re-designing any component involves significant engineering risk and expense.  I hate to say it, but it's not much of a gift to Ukraine.  I would bet that one of the defense startups like Andruil would have better luck designing a replacement that would be cheaper and much easier to manufacture with modern electronics, CPUs and software.

Given that ballistic missile interception at scale is a strategic necessity, replacing Patriot with a economic alternative is a priority for the US and its allies.

I think it’s naive to think that China isn’t a threat. I agree that China probably doesn’t want to invade and colonise Australia (but, who knows maybe if it was an easy thing to do because the US let them they would?). What they do want to do is to dictate to Japan, Australia and the Pacific. They want control. And more influence in the region would help them if they were to go to war with the US over Taiwan. Why else are they launching missiles over the pacific? 

PM Albanese and our great foreign minister Penny Wong are doing a good job of avoiding confrontation with China, while quietly securing Australia’s interests and independence. When China entered into a security agreement with the Solomon Islands it pretty much lost PM Morrison and the LNP (conservative party) the election. It made the LNP look extremely incompetent. So PM Albanese and Penny Wong would be aware of this domestic perception too. The pacific islands are the winners. They’re probably getting more out of Australia than they would without the competition from China. But, they’re not stupid, they know that Australia is more reliable and less threatening and more democratic than China, so they’d rather negotiate with and accept aid from us. Friendship and not being an authoritarian bully is Australia’s superpower. Someone should tell Trump that sometimes soft power wins the day over military might.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida

What we are seeing in the Pacific is the ripple effect of a retreating U.S. hegemony and increasingly ambiguous commitments to allies that once placed complete trust in the alliance. Middle powers like Australia and Japan, which traditionally relied on U.S. security guarantees, are now losing their strategic orientation in a multipolar world. Fear and uncertainty naturally come first.

Australia, in particular, feels increasingly alone as the only major Anglo-Saxon nation in the region besides NZ. China is stepping into Australia's comfort zone simply because it now can. That doesn't mean China views Australia as a primary threat—far from it. Japan is a bit more concerning for Beijing, although the balance of power still heavily favors China.

China's growing presence in the Pacific is all about military expansion. I think the Chinese leadership has also learned from Japan's failure in World War II. Much of what we see today is deterrence-building aimed primarily at the US in prep for any move against TW. I don't think sending a few Australian or Japanese warships would fundamentally change China's calculations.

Australia needs to learn from its Asian neighbors and decide whether it sees itself primarily as an Asia-Pacific nation or an Anglo-Saxon nation. The same question applies to Japan. Pragmatism has long been the key to how Asian civilization states have coexisted for millennia, and that lesson may become increasingly relevant in the years ahead.

I would like to see a reasonably faithful adaptation of the whole series.  I got to know the Ingalls family from the books, which my mother read to me before I knew there was a television series—and I only ever managed to watch a few episodes of that, finding them utterly unlike the stories in the books.  But I think we stopped after *By the Shores of Silver Lake*.  I think Mary's illness was too much for me to handle, and perhaps my mother sensed I wouldn't be as interested in Laura growing up in the later books, though seeing them on the shelf always intrigued me.

I disagree with the use of "novels" and "fiction" to describe the books.  Yes, the episodes were edited and no doubt the stories retold to bring together things that really happened at different times, the events simplified and told out of order—much as they might be in real-life reminiscences—but still basically truth.  Perhaps "fictionalized" would be a fairer description.

The original works contain truths that are uncomfortable today.  The pioneers weren't enlightened; they were afraid of the Indians and had reason to be, just as the Indians had reason to resent white settlers.  When Pa participated in a minstrel show, he didn't think he was doing anything to harm or demean black folks.  We cringe when we read these things today, but they were the realities with which the people of another age lived.  And they could be presented fairly, with context, by a sensitive adaptation.  That would be worth seeing.
