comments.body:
Greater ethnic diversity in television and film is, on balance, is a positive development. But when historical dramas begin rewriting the past in the name of present-day values, they risk replacing one false narrative with another.
What happens when future generations grow up watching new period dramas like Little House on the Prairie and Bridgerton and come away believing that 18th and 19th-century society was broadly inclusive? How are they supposed to grasp the depth of slavery, segregation, exclusion, and the everyday humiliations that minorities endured if those realities are softened, minimized, or simply written out of the story?
History isn't valuable because it's comforting. It's valuable because it's true. Sanitizing the past -- whether to make it more inclusive, more patriotic, or more politically convenient -- doesn't promote justice; it promotes historical amnesia.
The impulse to rewrite history isn't confined to one ideology. Whether it's Hollywood reshaping the past to reflect contemporary cultural values or politicians pressuring museums and public institutions to tell a more flattering national story, the result is the same: future generations inherit mythology instead of history. And a society that forgets what really happened is far more likely to repeat it.

comments.body: I'm the international coordinator for a large network of Congolese NGOs, most working on human rights, development and rule of law. A number of our organizations are involved in the Ebola response. We're trying to collaborate with the health authorities in the zones under government control, and fly under the radar in the zones under military occupation. Community members are so traumatized after many years of violence, occupation, and abandonment by their own government and the international community, that they have a hard time trusting the advice and actions of authorities - especially outsiders. This leads to attacks against the medical facilities and workers. We are doing what we can to gently explain how the virus works and what is needed to get it stopped. This is as much a psycho-social crisis as a medical crisis.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
The carbon cycle for the last 2 million years was doing 180-280ppm atmospheric CO2 over 10,000 years and we’ve done more change than that in 100 years. The speed of change now is much greater than virtually anything we have found in Earth’s climate history.

The last time CO2 went from 180-280ppm global temperature increased by around 4 degrees C and sea level rose 130 meters. (See graph below, 1) It takes time for temperature and sea level to equilibrate with elevated atmospheric CO2 and we could blow much further off of that graph.

One amplifying feedback alone out of dozens, loss of albedo or heat reflectivity from Arctic summer sea ice melt, over the last several decades has been equivalent to 25 percent of the climate forcing of anthropogenic CO2. And that will continue to increase as that ice largely disappears by mid century.

The Titanic sank because by the time the lookout called the warning the ship had too much momentum to turn. The Earth has a lot more momentum, e.g. we've already likely locked in at least 6 meters of sea level rise from the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and decade to decade warming in the near term is also virtually locked in.

That momentum is building and the higher we let global temperatures rise the greater the risk of them going really high as amplifying feedbacks strengthen.

1.  (graph of the last 400,000 years of global temperature, CO2 and sea level https://www.ces.fau.edu/nasa/images/impacts/slr-co2-temp-400000yrs.jpg )

comments.name: Christopher Nation
comments.body: A significant problem with sea temps around Britain is the shallowness of the waters. For some years now signs of human habitation have been dredged up from the North Sea off East Anglia. The 'land bridge' between Britain and what is now the coast of Europe, was dry land, now known a 'Doggerland' after the Dogger Bank,. Its average depth is around 15 to 20 meters (about 50–65 feet), with some parts as shallow as 13 meters. Sustained high temps will heat up this water considerably added to which the North Sea is somewhat akin to a marine lake. The waters that drain out of it down the English Channel run back 6 hours later.

comments.name: Metaphor
comments.body:
So if I may quibble a bit, are the oceans getting hotter or are they getting warmer? I mean, for something to be getting hotter it sort of has to be hot to begin with. It's like saying that when water boiling at 100 Celsius lowers its temperature to 99 Celsius it is getting "colder." I guarantee that if you stick your hand in 99 Celsius water you are going to get a nasty burn from water that is "colder" than 100 Celsius, in which case it hardly seems appropriate to compare 99 to 100 and say that the former is "colder" than the latter.

I suppose my point is that human-caused climate change is undeniable, but when the news media are careless with their use of language it only gives support to climate deniers who see nothing but hysteria in the media's reporting on climate change.

Thanks for reporting on this subject. It's sad to see the terrible effect on sea life from these ocean heat waves. And this ocean heat has other grave implications.

There are parts of the system that are already out of our hands. And those parts are related to the ocean. Because we know that we’ve already put a lot of heat content into the ocean. 

And in the case of the Antarctic Ice Sheet, regarding the marine based ice which is very sensitive to ocean temperatures—West Antarctica 3.3 meters of sea level rise equivalent of ice, East Antarctica 19 meters—we are committed to some response of the ice sheet to the heat that has already gone into the ocean. And Greenland has around 3 meters worth of marine based ice as well.

How much response? According to the paleoclimate record at 1.5-2°C above preindustrial temperature around 6-9 meters of sea level rise (we’re likely already committed to at least 2°C)
At 3°C, tens of meters eventually.

Times scales are the big question and the community in general has been conservative with time scales.

comments.body: Having just turned 60 in April I'm not only from a time before cell phones and camcorders but remember how we captured our daily lives with 16 mm film cameras and home movies and Polaroids and tape recorders. This was before we as a society turned the camera eye onto ourselves constantly and just lived for the moment and cherished the memories in our heads. I remember meeting with Ross back in 1985 as a 19 year old aspiring film critic and journalist when his classic Sherman's March premiered. I grew up loving the purity of cinema verite in high school and was lucky enough to know Frederick Wiseman and Barbara Koppel who were two of my favorites. The personal approach of Ross turning his camera onto his ex-girlfriends and family members seemed at the time so radical and unnerving in the same way that PBS documentary An American Family where we watched the Loud family disintegrate before our very eyes. I'm devastated about the loss of his son and his guilt over whatever role his filmmaking had on his family. But every artist--writers and filmmakers-- knows deep in their hearts that they use and consume their background and family members as fodder for their work. Like Truman Capote said in reaction to his infamous Esquire piece: " What did they expect? I'm  a writer,  and I use everything. "

comments.name: sadmar
comments.body:
The real pioneer of introspective filmmaking was Ed Pincus, who was McElwee's teacher at MIT. But Ross did not merely ape Pincus's confessional diary films. There's a level of irony in Sherman's March, hints that the first person address to the camera is as much performed as genuine, that McElwee is an unreliable narrator, and the idea he truly originally intended to make a film about Sherman is nonsense. (Fun trivia fact for documentary nerds: the narration at the beginning is voiced by Ricky Leacock.) Anyway, what McElwee certainly accomplished was adapting the diary form to films that had much broader appeal, played in theaters, got shown on PBS, had DVD releases. There's a reason Ed Pincus's work is not well known. It's too close to the bone.
Another documentary filmmaker who no doubt inspired McElwee to some extent is Michael Rubbo, who created the form of a film that unfolds out of the failure to complete some other ostensible project. Rubbo's Waiting for Fidel is most directly the template for Roger and Me, and Nick Broomfield's solo films, but along with Sherman's March they show that era had a current of filmmaker-as-character imbued with cheek.

It is disheartening to read that Ms. Zuñiga still appears to believe that Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro, or Delcy Rodríguez acted with the best of intentions.

Chávez’s daughter lives in a luxury apartment in New York City, owns multiple properties in Europe, and is among the wealthiest women connected to Venezuela’s ruling elite, with much of that wealth originated from misappropriated Venezuelan public funds. Swiss authorities have frozen approximately one billion dollars in assets linked to Maduro’s network, including cash and gold reserves. Imagine what could have been accomplished for ordinary Venezuelans with resources of that magnitude.

Instead, countless people were left in poorly constructed housing that, in many cases, was inadequately engineered and became a death sentence when disaster struck.

Anatoly, who has long defended Venezuela’s so-called socialist revolution, emphasizes racial inequities while minimizing the systemic neglect and pervasive corruption that characterized the construction of these housing projects. The self-proclaimed socialists were never committed to lifting the poor. Rather, they cultivated political dependence by keeping people reliant on state handouts, monitoring attendance at political rallies, voting through systems of coercion and intimidation, and encouraging citizens to report anyone who dared to think independently. Those are the hallmarks not of social justice, but of an authoritarian regime determined to perpetuate its own power.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
The ocean for many is out of sight and mind. But Atlantic fish stocks 10 years ago were between 1/1,000 and 1/10,000 of what they were just 150 to 200 years ago. (1) 

The continental shelves used to be forests of sponges and corals, critical habitat for fish development.

Trawling has reduced to mud, to parking lot, a greater area of the ocean floor than the area of forests cut down in the history of humanity.

Over hunting and fishing, habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and now climate change.

None of these things happen in a vacuum, but there are synergies among them which make the whole vastly greater than the sum of the parts.

We are a water planet and as goes the ocean go we.

1. Here’s a presentation by the Scripps Oceanographic Institute marine ecologist Jeremy Jackson where he discusses this and a lot more.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NyWHSflfiag

The lots instead appeared to have been “fraudulently diverted and sold into the marketplace in the United States,” it said. Mars added that it was working with the authorities to find out how the food came to be sold,..." So not Mars but their vendor contracted to destroy the food....but instead sold it!!!

So I have three issues...the first is with the article itself, which shows a picture of the wrong food...not the canned food involved in the recall...second, VCA...I have had two different pets saved by the vets at our VCA, with one pet treated during COVID when many vet offices remained closed in our city. comments.name: Jay E. Simkin
comments.body:
Weeks before Allied forces landed in Normandy (D-Day, 6 June 1944), they air-dropped arms to resistance units. Chief among these: single-shot, sheet-metal "Liberator" pistols. These were to be used to attack a Nazi soldier and to take his weapon. 

Iran cannot be invaded: its core is ringed with forested mountains (e.g. Zagros) and vast deserts. These obstacles mean an invader's supply lines will be long and exposed to attack by guerillas. 

Only Iranians can oust a regime that has murdered many and subjected most of the rest to decades of grinding poverty. Iranians have repeatedly protested against their brutal regime. They've been met with lethal force. 

So, Iranians must be armed. Pistols - with spare magazines and a 50-round box of ammunition - should be air-dropped, at night, into all major cities. The police will seize some: that does not matter. 

But rank-and-file residents will get some. So, if they choose to attack the regime's enforcers - the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and their street-level thugs, the basiji - they can do so. This is the only way to give Iranians a chance to free themselves. 

If they don't take action, then we prepare for a decades-long war of containment. The U.S. and its allies contained the Soviet Union for 70 years, until it collapsed (1989-90). 

Iran, under its clerico-military regime, is no less malevolent. There can be no peace treaty with rabid, die-hard haters. To think otherwise is delusion.

comments.body:
Regarding the Mayor's bus plan-

Bus riders need more bus capacity, more frequent buses and more bus routes – bus lanes are not “the solution” if there are no buses.

Buses are slowed due to DOT red lights and reduced speed limit.

Buses are slowed for various rider reasons especially riders with canes, walkers, wheelchairs, shopping carts, strollers.

Buses are slowed when they are packed and people can’t get on or off.

Getting rid of bus stops actually makes a longer “trip” overall - because riders need to walk further to get the bus.

In fact, the Mayor’s “plan” is really bad for people with mobility issues – the people who really depend on buses.

A bus ride that is 5 minutes "faster" is not helpful if you need to walk more blocks to get to the bus, wait in the rain 20 minutes for the bus and the bus is packed when it arrives

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen

Many people are upset about migration and inflation. However many people are unaware that climate change is an increasing driver of both. By voting for right wing politicians who deny climate science they are working to make climate change impacts worse, driving even more migration and inflation.

Many people think that today’s migrations and high prices are due only to political or economic policy, missing the underlying catalyst: climate change. 

Extreme weather, prolonged droughts, and crop failures are driving global migration as unlivable conditions force millions from their homes. 

Simultaneously, these same climate shocks trigger "climateflation." Scorched agricultural land and collapsing supply chains drive up the cost of everything from food to insurance. 

Connecting these dots shows that migration and inflation are some of the  symptoms of a heating planet.

comments.name: Michael D from Victoria, BC
comments.body: As an alternative, how about reading novels that were actually written during the 1960s?  An obvious suggestion would be James Michener's "The Drifters".  Published in 1971, it nevertheless captures and weaves together multiple threads from the late 1960s.  I first read it in 1978, when - much like the characters in the novel - I was hitchhiking around Europe.  We actually went out of our way to make a brief visit to Torremolinos, where so much of the novel takes place.  When I reread it now, it evokes both that era and my own youth in a way that a recently-written historical novel cannot.
